reason: The text strongly emphasizes hierarchy through multiple structural elements: (1) Kings are presented as central authority figures who command others—the King of Israel directs his servants, summons and commands prophets (400 of them), and orders officials. Jehoshaphat addresses him with deference despite being a fellow king. (2) There is a clear chain of command: prophets respond to royal summons, officials execute the king's orders regarding Micaiah's imprisonment, and military personnel answer to the king. (3) The passage repeatedly identifies individuals by their hierarchical rank (King of Israel, King of Judah, servants, prophets, official/saris). (4) Even when Micaiah speaks truth against the king's wishes, he does so while ultimately subject to the king's authority—he can be struck, imprisoned, and restricted by royal order. The entire narrative structure presumes and displays hierarchical relationships as the organizing principle of political and religious life.
